blocks.md: A cache is a small, fast copy of data that is expensive to fetch. Keep the **most recently used** entries inside a strict byte budget so repeated reads avoid the backing store.

blocks.label: FIG 1
blocks.caption: A hit skips the backing store. A miss fetches once, admits the value if it fits, and returns a copy.

blocks.title: The invariant
blocks.md: After every operation, `UsedBytes` is at most the configured capacity. Count both value bytes and `contract.PerEntryMetadataBytes`; capacity is about accounted memory, not entry count.

blocks.input:
capacity = 2 entries
Put(A), Put(B), Get(A), Put(C)
blocks.explain: `Get(A)` makes A newest. When C arrives, B is the oldest entry, so B leaves. Use a map for lookup plus an ordered recency list for constant-time movement.

items: `Get` and `Put` refresh recency; replacement counts as a fresh use.
Copy values on both input and output so caller mutation cannot change cached data.
An entry that cannot fit is not admitted; a zero-capacity cache stores nothing.
Evict the oldest entries until the new value fits, never after admitting it.

items.title: Make accounting exact
items.md: Centralize each entry's charged size and update it on insert, replacement, and eviction.

items.title: Separate lookup from order
items.md: Use one structure to find a key and another to move that entry to the newest position.

items.title: Optimize after correctness
items.md: A linear list can pass semantics; constant-time recency maintenance improves `metadata_work`.

blocks.title: What the score is saying
blocks.md: Fewer `backing_reads` means the policy retained useful data. Lower `metadata_work` means the same decisions required less bookkeeping. Correctness is always the gate.
